    HR 2302 ENR: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr2302enr

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 2302 (Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025) revokes Public Land Order 3309 and directs the Secretary of the Interior to place approximately 80 acres of BLM land and approximately 185 acres of Indian Creek Ranch land into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians within 180 days of enactment, subject to valid existing rights. The Act directs a review to determine whether a survey is required, declares the trust land part of the Tribe's reservation, and provides that it may not be used for class II or class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    107 HR 2306 RS: Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr2306rs

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 2306 (Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act), as reported in the Senate by Mr. Lee with an amendment on November 12, 2026, amends section 2406(l) of Public Law 116-9 and Public Law 107-62 to extend the authority of the Adams Memorial Commission through 2033. The reported text locates the Adams Memorial within the area depicted as 'Adams Memorial: Eligible Additional Area' on a map dated February 25, 2025, and requires that the final design be approved by a majority of the Commission, including specified appointed members, before it is authorized. The amendment also repeals Sections 2 and 3 of Public Law 107-315. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    HR 2400 ENR: Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr2400enr

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 2400 (Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026) directs the Secretary of Agriculture to transfer administrative jurisdiction over approximately 557 acres of Forest Service land, known as the Four Corners Federal land, to the Secretary of the Interior, and directs that the land be taken into trust for the Pit River Tribe, subject to valid existing rights. The Act excludes approximately 87 acres of roads, highways, rights-of-way, easements, and special use permit areas, requires a complete survey within 180 days of enactment, and declares the land part of the Tribe's reservation. The land may not be used for class II or class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 2876 PCS: University of Utah Research Park Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr2876pcs

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 2876 (University of Utah Research Park Act) passed the House of Representatives on December 15, 2025, and was received in the Senate and placed on the calendar on November 16, 2026. The bill confirms that the University of Utah's use of approximately 593.54 acres of non-Federal land in Salt Lake City, conveyed under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act by patent 43-99-0012, as a university research park is a valid public purpose, subject to the terms of the 1970 Department of the Interior letter and related approvals. It also confirms as valid public purposes other uses consistent with a research park and related university purposes, including student housing and a transit hub. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    HR 7834 ENR: Safe Cloud Storage Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr7834enr

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 7834 (Safe Cloud Storage Act) adds section 202 to Title II of the PROTECT Our Children Act of 2008, limiting civil claims and criminal charges against approved cloud service providers that store child pornography, child obscenity, or intimate visual depictions of minors under contracts with law enforcement or prosecutorial agencies, except in cases of specified intentional, negligent, or otherwise defined misconduct. The section sets requirements for approved vendors, including security consistent with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, annual independent audits under NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5, data stored in the United States unless the contracting agency consents to transfer, and a notification letter to the Department of Justice. The Act also specifies evidence retention rules for covered agencies and adds a clerical amendment to the Act's table of contents. BILLS-SEL-01

    119 HR 8705 RH: Civics and History Advancement to Restore Learning, Integrity, and Education Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8705rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8705 (Civics and History Advancement to Restore Learning, Integrity, and Education Act, or the CHARLIE Act), introduced by Mr. Owens on May 7, 2026, and reported with an amendment by the House Committee on Education and Workforce on November 18, 2026, amends section 2231 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965. The amendment prohibits funds made available under the American history and civics subpart from being used for discriminatory equity ideology or gender ideology, as defined by reference to Executive Orders 14190 and 14168. It also bars the Secretary from giving grant priority to an eligible entity on the basis of race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status. BILLS-SEL-01

    119 HR 9381 RH: AI Workforce Assessment and Research Enhancement Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9381rh

    FAPD-AI: The AI Workforce Assessment and Research Enhancement Act, or the AWARE Act, as reported with an amendment in the House, amends the Act of March 4, 1913 (29 U.S.C. 2) to require the Bureau of Labor Statistics to collect full and complete statistics on the usage of artificial intelligence in conditions of labor and in products and distribution. Collection must begin no later than 18 months after enactment, and artificial intelligence is defined by reference to section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020. The bill's findings state that existing Bureau of Labor Statistics programs were not designed to measure employer adoption of AI, worker-level use, or related workforce effects on a timely basis. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    119 S1682 RS: Alex Gate Safety Act of 2025 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s1682rs

    FAPD-AI: The Alex Gate Safety Act of 2026, as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation with an amendment, directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to promulgate within 180 days of enactment final consumer product safety standards consisting of ASTM F900–25, ASTM F1184–23e1, and ASTM F2200–24 as in effect on the date of enactment. It requires organizations that revise those standards to notify the Commission, with revisions treated as Commission-adopted standards after 180 days unless the Commission determines within 90 days that the revision does not improve safety. The bill also directs the Commission to conduct a national public awareness campaign within 2 years of enactment and to submit a report to Congress within 3 years. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 23:55:16 Eastern time ET
    119 S1885 RS: Stop the Scroll Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s1885rs

    FAPD-AI: The Stop the Scroll Act, as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation with an amendment, requires the Federal Trade Commission, with the concurrence of the Secretary of Health and Human Services acting through the Surgeon General, to implement a mental health warning label on covered platforms, defined to include social media platforms and anonymous content sharing platforms. Under the bill, a covered label must be displayed each time a user accesses a covered platform from within the United States, must warn of potential negative mental health impacts, must provide access to federal resources including the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and must be redisplayed after each hour of continued use. The bill directs the Commission to promulgate implementing regulations within 180 days, authorizes enforcement by the Commission and by state attorneys general, and the source text provided is truncated. BILLS-SEL-01

    91 S4950 RS: Institute for Telecommunication Sciences Codification Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s4950rs

    FAPD-AI: The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences Codification Act, or the ITS Codification Act, as reported by the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation with an amendment, adds section 106 to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration Organization Act to establish the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences as a test center operated by the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information. The section designates the Institute as the primary laboratory for the executive branch on radio frequency emissions, spectrum propagation, and Federal and non-Federal spectrum sharing, and transfers the emergency communication and tracking technologies research initiative from the National Institute of Standards and Technology to the Institute. The section also requires a report to Congress within 18 months of enactment on the status of that initiative. BILLS-SEL-01

    Wells v. Secretary of Health and Human Services (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cofc-1_24-vv-01264 / USCOURTS-cofc-1_24-vv-01264-0

    FAPD-AI: In a dismissal decision filed September 16, 2026 and reissued for public availability November 13, 2026, Special Master Herbrina D.S. Young dismissed the petition of Kathie Wells, filed on behalf of her minor child C.B. under the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. The petition alleged injuries following MMR and Tdap vaccines administered October 6, 2023. The special master found that the petitioner did not file an expert report or a substitution of counsel by the court-ordered deadline, and that the medical records were insufficient to prove the claim, so the case was dismissed for failure to prosecute and for insufficient proof. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Branstetter v. USA (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01250 / USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01250-0

    FAPD-AI: In an order filed November 13, 2026, Judge Ryan T. Holte of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims dismissed without prejudice the complaint of pro se plaintiff Jadi Branstetter under Rule 41(b) of the Rules of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims for failure to prosecute. The order states that the plaintiff had not paid the filing fee or submitted a completed in forma pauperis application by the October 18, 2026 deadline set in the court's September 18, 2026 order. The Clerk was directed to enter judgment dismissing the complaint. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_25-cv-00225 / USCOURTS-cit-1_25-cv-00225-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion dated November 16, 2026, Judge Gary S. Katzmann of the U.S. Court of International Trade denied the Motion for Judgment on the Agency Record filed by Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. and the related motion filed by plaintiff-intervenors Colakoglu. The court held that the Department of Commerce's selection of a land valuation benchmark, a Colliers International report rather than a Cushman & Wakefield report, is supported by substantial evidence. The case concerns Commerce's administrative review of the countervailing duty order on Turkish rebar for the 2022 period of review, in which the value of a rent-free government land lease was determined. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Louis Poulsen A/S v. Lightzey (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02048 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02048-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order decided November 17, 2026, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the Northern District of Illinois denial of attorney fees under 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a) in Louis Poulsen A/S v. Lightzey, No. 25-2048. The court found no abuse of discretion in the district court's conclusion that the case was not exceptional, after Lightzey was voluntarily dismissed from a Schedule A trademark suit for lack of personal jurisdiction. The court declined to address two law professor amici's concerns about Schedule A litigation generally. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca8-25-02555 / USCOURTS-ca8-25-02555-0

    FAPD-AI: A letter dated November 17, 2026 from the Eighth Circuit Clerk of Court, Susan E. Bindler, notified counsel in United States v. Phillip Keith, No. 25-2555, that the court issued an opinion and entered judgment. The letter reminds counsel that petitions for rehearing and rehearing en banc must be received within 14 days of the entry of judgment, must be filed electronically through CM/ECF, and are subject to denial as untimely if not received within that period. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:52 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Angelo Scott (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca8-26-02342 / USCOURTS-ca8-26-02342-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 17, 2026, the Eighth Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Iowa revocation of supervised release and sentence of time served plus 36 months of supervised release for Angelo Lavell Scott, No. 26-2342. The court held that the district court did not abuse its discretion in imposing a 60-day location monitoring condition or the new supervised release term. The court also granted appointed counsel's motion to withdraw. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:51 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Ivan Baez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-03175 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-03175-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential opinion in No. 25-3175, the Third Circuit affirmed a 262-month sentence imposed on Ivan Nicholas Baez for sexual exploitation of a minor. The court held that Pennsylvania harassment convictions were not similar to disorderly conduct or disturbing the peace under U.S.S.G. § 4A1.2(c), so the district court properly assigned criminal history points for them. The court also held that any error in counting those points would not have been plain. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:51 Eastern time ET
    Mamdouh Hebishy v. Attorney General United States of America (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01765 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01765-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion in No. 26-1765, the Third Circuit denied a pro se petition for review filed by Mamdouh Hebishy, an Egyptian citizen challenging the Board of Immigration Appeals' denial of his third motion to reopen. The court concluded that the BIA did not abuse its discretion in finding the motion time- and number-barred, as the evidence showed Coptic Christian conditions in Egypt had persisted rather than materially changed. The court stated that it lacked jurisdiction to review the BIA's refusal to reopen sua sponte. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:51 Eastern time ET
    In re: Jair Ramirez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-02816 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-02816-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion in No. 26-2816, the Third Circuit denied a pro se petition for a writ of mandamus filed by Jair Ramirez, a Colombian citizen, which asked the court to compel the Western District of Pennsylvania to rule on his 28 U.S.C. § 2241 habeas petition challenging ICE detention. The court found no undue delay because a magistrate judge had issued a report and recommendation on October 13, 2026, and parties could still file objections. The court also denied Ramirez's motion to expedite as moot. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    In re: Catherine Wakefield (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-03198 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-03198-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential per curiam opinion filed November 17, 2026, the Third Circuit denied Catherine Wakefield's pro se petition for a writ of mandamus. The court found the petition moot because the District of New Jersey had already denied the pending requests for injunctive relief, and it stated that federal appellate courts lack authority to direct state courts in her New Jersey divorce proceedings.   • Observed at 22:09:51 Eastern time ET
    Meng Huang v. OSU, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03903 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03903-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonrecommended opinion, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Ohio judgment in Huang v. The Ohio State University, No. 25-3903, after a second trial in which the jury found for the defendants on Title VII and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims. The court held that Huang forfeited her challenge to the jury interrogatory on employee status by failing to object, and it found her remaining challenges regarding exclusion of survey evidence and limits on economic damages argument unpersuasive. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:50 Eastern time ET
    Yoan Aguiar-Fernandez, et al v. U.S. Attorney General (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-12318 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-12318-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion in No. 24-12318, the Eleventh Circuit held that Cuban nationals released from immigration detention under 8 U.S.C. § 1226 conditional parole are not eligible for adjustment of status under the Cuban Adjustment Act, which requires humanitarian parole under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(d)(5)(A). The Aguiar-Fernandez family had applied under the Act after being released on recognizance citing § 1226, and an immigration judge found them ineligible, a ruling the Board of Immigration Appeals summarily affirmed. The court denied the petition for review. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:50 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Lucy Carrillo Gonzalez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-11365 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-11365-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion in No. 25-11365, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed a 48-month sentence imposed on Lucy Carrillo Gonzalez for her role in a cocaine distribution conspiracy. The court found no clear error in the district court's inclusion of November 2023 cocaine sales as relevant conduct, its application of the U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12) premises enhancement, and its denial of a minimal-role reduction under § 3B1.2(a). The court also found no abuse of discretion in the sentence's substantive reasonableness. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:50 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Jason Cain (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02721 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02721-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion filed November 17, 2026, in No. 25-2721, the Third Circuit reversed a district court order that suppressed evidence recovered from electronic devices in a child sexual abuse material prosecution of Jason Cain, and remanded for further proceedings. The court held that the good-faith exception applied to the first search warrant, which was issued by a magistrate and authorized a search for images of two named victims rather than child pornography. The court further held that the officers' reliance on that warrant extended to the second, third, and fourth warrants. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-08043 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-08043-0

    FAPD-AI: In this published opinion filed November 17, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, in an opinion by Judge Hartz, affirmed the District of Wyoming's denial of the defendant's motions to suppress methamphetamine seized from a Volkswagen during a traffic stop and search. The court held that officers had probable cause under the automobile exception and the collective-knowledge doctrine, based on a confidential informant's tips that were substantially corroborated by controlled buys, GPS tracking, and the vehicle's observed mechanical problems. The opinion states that the defendant's sentence of 300 months' imprisonment was not challenged on appeal, and that only the denial of the suppression motions was at issue. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Adetayo v. Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-09526 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-09526-0

    FAPD-AI: In this unpublished order and judgment filed November 17, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, panel Bacharach, McHugh, and Carson, addressed a pro se petition for review by Banjoko Olakitan Adetayo of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision and an order of removal to Nigeria. The court dismissed the challenge to detention as moot after the petitioner was removed, and denied the petition as to the order of removal because the due process claims were unexhausted and did not fall within the constitutional exception, while retaining jurisdiction based on collateral consequences. The court granted the petitioner's motion to proceed in forma pauperis. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:48 Eastern time ET
    Lands, et al v. Federal Emergency Management Agency, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-02103 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-02103-0

    FAPD-AI: In this published opinion filed November 17, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, in an opinion by Judge Ebel, consolidated appeals from the District of New Mexico in Lands, et al v. Federal Emergency Management Agency, et al, which challenged FEMA's interpretation of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon Fire Assistance Act as not providing noneconomic damages. The court held that the Act does not clearly and unequivocally waive the United States' sovereign immunity for noneconomic damages claims, reversed the district court's contrary decision, and remanded for further proceedings. The opinion also notes that FEMA's motion for expedited resolution was granted in light of the finite funding available under the Act. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 22:09:48 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Trujillo (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-02124 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-02124-0

    FAPD-AI: In this published opinion filed November 17, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, in an opinion by Judge Phillips, affirmed a 70-month sentence imposed by the District of New Mexico on Daniel Jesus Trujillo for illegal reentry under 8 U.S.C. § 1326. The court held that the 10-level enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2L1.2(b)(2)(A) applies because the maximum 15-year sentence for a prior New Mexico armed-robbery conviction, minus suspended time, exceeded five years, even though actual incarceration was less than five years and New Mexico probation credit is not incarceration time. The opinion explains the guideline definitions of "sentence imposed" and "sentence of imprisonment" in §§ 2L1.2 and 4A1.2 and the procedural history of the sentencing. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Sean Nealy v. John Phelan (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-25-05175 / USCOURTS-caDC-25-05175-0

    FAPD-AI: In Nealy v. Phelan, the D.C. Circuit affirmed a district court judgment upholding a Navy disability rating assigned to Navy veteran Sean Nealy, who has post-traumatic stress disorder. The Physical Disability Board of Review had recommended a six-month temporary fifty-percent rating followed by a permanent ten-percent rating, and the court found that the Navy lawfully and reasonably applied the relevant statute. The opinion was argued September 8, 2026 and decided November 17, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:28 Eastern time ET
    Western Towboat Company v. NOAA, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-25-05415 / USCOURTS-caDC-25-05415-0

    FAPD-AI: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam judgment on November 17, 2026, affirming the district court's dismissal of Western Towboat Company's suit against the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The court held that NOAA's charging decision and its referral of the matter to an EPA administrative law judge are not final agency action reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, and that the due process claim rests on speculative future injury. The case arose from a steel drydock that capsized and sank in the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary while being transported by Western, for which NOAA charged Western alone under the National Marine Sanctuaries Act after its co-respondents settled. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:27 Eastern time ET
    Xiaomi v. Advanced Standard Comm (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-10735 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-10735-0

    FAPD-AI: In Xiaomi, Inc. v. Advanced Standard Communication, L.L.C., the Fifth Circuit reversed a Northern District of Texas order granting Xiaomi discovery under 28 U.S.C. § 1782 for use in a Unified Patent Court proceeding. The court held that the district court applied an incorrect standard under Intel factor two and did not analyze Intel factor three at the level of granularity presented by the parties. Upon rebalancing the Intel factors, the court concluded that they weigh against ordering discovery at the present time, and the opinion is not designated for publication. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:27 Eastern time ET
    Mateo Mateo-Miguel v. Todd Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-03138 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-03138-0

    FAPD-AI: In Mateo-Miguel v. Blanche, the Sixth Circuit denied a petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision that denied a Guatemalan citizen's applications for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture. The court held that the BIA's adverse credibility determination and its finding of insufficient corroboration were supported by substantial evidence, citing inconsistencies in the petitioner's testimony regarding his ability to speak Spanish and details of the alleged incidents. The opinion is not recommended for publication. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:27 Eastern time ET
    Laura Obergefell v. Firelands Regional Medical Center, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-03306 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-03306-0

    FAPD-AI: In Obergefell v. Firelands Regional Medical Center, the Sixth Circuit affirmed a Northern District of Ohio judgment awarding $5,261.80 in deposition transcript costs to the prevailing defendant in an age discrimination action. The court found no abuse of discretion in the district court's rejection of the plaintiff's arguments regarding case complexity, chilling effect, the winning party's conduct, and the defendant's operating profits. The court also denied the plaintiff's motion to supplement the appellate record. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:26 Eastern time ET
    Nathaniel Jackson v. Michael Gilday (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-02076 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-02076-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fourth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the district court's grant of qualified immunity to Navy officials in Jackson v. Gilday, No. 25-2076. Jackson, a former Air Force airman confined at the Naval Consolidated Brig Charleston, sued under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act over a delayed beard-grooming waiver that resulted in disciplinary action and solitary confinement. The court held that Jackson had not shown the law was clearly established, citing the requirement of fair warning under Tolan v. Cotton. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:26 Eastern time ET
    US v. Samuel Oakley, Jr. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-04171 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-04171-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fourth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the conviction and sentence of Samuel McCoy Oakley, Jr., in United States v. Oakley, No. 25-4171, for drug-related offenses. The court held that Oakley waived his guilty plea challenges by withdrawing his pro se motion to withdraw the plea, and that his appeal waiver was valid despite an imperfect Rule 11 colloquy, so his sentencing arguments fell within the waiver's scope and were not reviewable. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:26 Eastern time ET
    US v. Joseph Dadisman (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-04652 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-04652-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fourth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the district court's denial of suppression on remand in United States v. Dadisman, No. 25-4652. Dadisman had pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute more than 50 grams of methamphetamine and was sentenced to 136 months' imprisonment. The court held that the district court permissibly resolved a factual dispute and credited the officers' testimony over Dadisman's, establishing reasonable suspicion for the prolonged traffic stop, and that it did not abuse its discretion by declining to take additional evidence. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    USA v. Hall (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-20501 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-20501-0

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the sentence in United States v. Hall, No. 25-20501, following David Michael Hall's guilty plea to two counts of bank robbery. For the first time on appeal, Hall argued that his prior Texas state robbery conviction did not qualify him as a career offender under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.1. The court affirmed because Hall conceded that his arguments were foreclosed by United States v. Williams, 184 F.4th 757 (5th Cir. 2026). USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:41:26 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Keelen (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-30111 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-30111-0

    FAPD-AI: In United States v. Keelen, the Fifth Circuit addressed Miguel Keelen's appeal of his conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) and fourteen conditions of supervised release. The court did not reach his Second Amendment and Commerce Clause challenges, which it noted are foreclosed by circuit precedent. It held that the district court's oral reference to the standard conditions of supervised release referred to the presentence report and satisfied the pronouncement requirement, and it affirmed in part and vacated and remanded in part. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119–140 (H.R. 1703, Choices for Increased Mobility Act of 2026), approved November 10, 2026, adds paragraph (24) to section 1834(a) of the Social Security Act concerning manual wheelchairs under Medicare Part B. For ultralightweight manual wheelchairs furnished on or after January 1, 2028, the Secretary must establish two or more HCPCS codes distinguishing bases made with titanium or carbon fiber from bases made without those materials. For titanium or carbon fiber based wheelchairs, payment to the supplier follows the usual amount under the subsection, the supplier may charge the beneficiary the difference between its actual charge and that payment, and the Secretary may require the supplier to issue a notice before purchase or rental.     Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-119publ142

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119–142 (H.R. 7730 / S. 3977, Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act), approved November 10, 2026, amends section 1182(1) of title 11, United States Code, to set the small business debtor limit at aggregate noncontingent liquidated debts of not more than $7,500,000, excluding debts owed to affiliates or insiders, with at least 50 percent arising from commercial or business activities. It excludes affiliated debtor groups above that limit, corporations subject to Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements, and their affiliates. It also amends section 109(e) of title 11 to set the chapter 13 individual debt limit at less than $2,750,000 and applies to cases commenced on or after the date of enactment. PLAW-SEL-01

    Don Young Doug Lamalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2026-11-17 / CREC-2026-11-17-pt1-PgH6236-8

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 7954, the Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, under suspension of the rules. The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations on buffalo and buffalo habitat through contracts, grants, and technical assistance, authorizes agreements to transfer surplus buffalo from Federal land to Indian land, and requires the Secretary to protect culturally sensitive or confidential tribal information. The authority provided by the bill ceases to be effective 7 years after enactment. CREC-SEL-01

    Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2026-11-17 / CREC-2026-11-17-pt1-PgH6238

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 8195, the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026, under suspension of the rules. The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to issue regulations establishing regional management frameworks for double-crested cormorants in coordination with the four Regional Flyway Councils. The bill requires population surveys and framework updates every 5 years, annual public reporting of take, and has no force or effect beginning January 1, 2034. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Senate resumed consideration of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a reconciliation bill, with the pending Thune (for Graham) amendment No. 2360 in the nature of a substitute and a Schumer motion to appeal the Chair's ruling on a point of order under section 313(b)(1)(E) of the Congressional Budget Act. Senator Schumer stated that the bill would reduce Medicaid and SNAP benefits, raise electricity costs, and increase the federal debt, and announced that Democratic senators would offer amendments during the vote-a-rama. Senator Thune stated that extending the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act provisions would prevent tax increases for families earning less than $400,000 and for pass-through businesses, and cited Congressional Budget Office revenue estimates for that act.     FAPD-AI: SA 2670, submitted by Mrs. Shaheen for herself and Ms. Collins, would strike section 70523 of H.R. 1 and insert requirements for cost-sharing on certain insulin products. For plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, group health plans and health insurance issuers would be required to cover selected insulin products without a deductible and with cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply through 2026, then at the lesser of $35 or 25 percent of the net negotiated price beginning in 2027. The amendment adds parallel provisions to the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, the Internal Revenue Code, and the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, and the text is truncated before its end. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: SA 2704, submitted by Ms. Ernst for herself, Mr. Grassley, Ms. Murkowski, and Ms. Collins, would strike sections 70512 and 70513 of H.R. 1 and insert new provisions on the clean electricity production credit. For wind and solar facilities, it sets a phase-out percentage that multiplies the credit: 60 percent for facilities whose construction begins in 2026, 20 percent for those beginning in 2027, and 0 percent for those beginning after December 31, 2027. It also restricts the credit for facilities using material assistance from prohibited foreign entities and adds definitions of specified foreign entities and foreign-influenced entities to section 7701(a), and the text is truncated before its end. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Lee submitted amendment SA 2724 to H.R. 1, which was ordered to lie on the table. The amendment would add the Regulations from the Executive in Need of Scrutiny Act of 2025 by replacing chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, with congressional review procedures for agency rules. These procedures include agency reports to each House of Congress and the Comptroller General before a rule takes effect, a joint resolution of approval procedure for major rules, and provisions on judicial review and private rights of action. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Scott of South Carolina, with Senator Tillis, submitted amendment SA 2759 to H.R. 1, which was ordered to lie on the table. The amendment would change the eligibility threshold in section 1400Z-1(c)(1)(A) of the Internal Revenue Code for Opportunity Zones from 70 percent to 80 percent. It would also add a section permitting transfers of excess health assets from section 401(h) health benefits accounts to pension plans to fund active employee benefits, subject to specified use, vesting, and cost requirements.     FAPD-AI: Senator Grassley submitted amendment SA 2789 to H.R. 1, which was ordered to lie on the table, proposing a chapter titled 'Pharmacy Benefit Manager Transparency'. The text would make unlawful specified pricing, reimbursement, and clawback practices by pharmacy benefit managers and the reporting of knowingly false information to federal agencies. It would also require pharmacy benefit managers to file annual reports with the Commission and the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and require the Commission and the Comptroller General to submit reports to Congress.     Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-26 / CREC-2025-06-26-pt1-PgH2984-6

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 875, the Jeremy and Angel Seay and Sergeant Brandon Mendoza Protect Our Communities from DUIs Act of 2025, which amends Sections 212(a)(2) and 237(a)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to make aliens convicted of, or who admit to, offenses for driving while intoxicated or impaired inadmissible and deportable, regardless of whether the offense is classified as a misdemeanor or felony. Representative Moore of Alabama, the sponsor, and Representative Raskin of Maryland presented remarks in support and in opposition, respectively, during the one-hour debate under House Resolution 530.     FAPD-AI: At the request of Senator Daines, the Senate Record printed a June 25, 2025 Government Accountability Office decision (File B-337163) on whether the Bureau of Land Management's Miles City Field Office Record of Decision and Approved Resource Management Plan Amendment is a rule under the Congressional Review Act (CRA). GAO concludes that the Miles City RMPA meets the Administrative Procedure Act definition of a rule, that no CRA exception applies, and that it is therefore subject to CRA submission requirements. The decision notes that the Interior Department did not submit a CRA report on the amendment, which allocates 1,745,040 acres as unavailable for further coal leasing consideration. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: At the request of Senator Sullivan, the Senate Record printed GAO decision B-337200, dated June 25, 2025, on whether the Bureau of Land Management's Central Yukon Record of Decision and Approved Resource Management Plan is a rule under the Congressional Review Act. GAO concludes that the Central Yukon RMP meets the APA definition of a rule, that none of the three CRA exceptions applies, and that it is therefore subject to CRA review. The decision states that Interior did not submit a CRA report and that the plan, approved November 12, 2024, provides management direction for 13.3 million acres of BLM-managed public lands in Alaska's Central Yukon planning area.     FAPD-AI: Senator Shaheen submitted amendment SA 2561 to H.R. 1 (as modified by SA 2360), proposing to strike section 70523 and insert new Public Health Service Act section 2799A-11, with parallel provisions in ERISA section 726 and Internal Revenue Code section 9826. The provisions require group health plans and health insurance issuers to cover selected insulin products without a deductible for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and to limit cost-sharing to $35 per 30-day supply, or from 2027 to the lesser of $35 or 25 percent of the net negotiated price. The amendment also applies the insulin requirements to qualified health plans and catastrophic plans under Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act section 1302, and it was ordered to lie on the table. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Curtis submitted amendment SA 2583 to H.R. 1 (as modified by SA 2360), proposing to strike section 70512 and insert revised provisions on the clean electricity production credit under Internal Revenue Code section 45Y. The amendment terminates the credit for wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, and denies the credit for qualified facilities whose construction includes material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity, as well as for taxpayers that are specified or foreign-influenced entities. It also adds definitions of prohibited foreign entity, specified foreign entity, and foreign-influenced entity to section 7701(a), and it was ordered to lie on the table. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Booker submitted amendment SA 2598 to H.R. 1 (as modified by SA 2360), proposing a new Chapter 7 titled "Respect, Advancement, and Increasing Support for Educators Act of 2025" or the "RAISE Act of 2025". The chapter adds Internal Revenue Code section 36C, a teacher tax credit of $1,000 for eligible educators plus an applicable amount of up to $14,000 ($9,000 for early childhood educators without a bachelor's degree) scaled by the student poverty ratio of qualifying schools above 39 percent, with inflation adjustments for taxable years beginning after 2026. The chapter also directs the Secretary of Education to collect school information, prohibits reducing teacher pay or teacher loan forgiveness because of the credit, and sets limitations on employers that engage in collective bargaining, and it was ordered to lie on the table. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Bennet submitted amendment SA 2646 to H.R. 1 (as modified by SA 2360), proposing to strike section 70120 and insert a new Internal Revenue Code section 275(b) that disallows deductions for disallowed foreign real property taxes, limits deductions for specified taxes to $10,000 ($5,000 for married individuals filing separately), and limits deductions for pass-through entity taxes using a threshold based on the greater of $40,000 ($20,000 for married individuals filing separately) or 50 percent of such taxes. The amendment also revises Internal Revenue Code sections 216, 702, 703, and 704 concerning the treatment of partnership and S corporation taxes, the definition of pass-through entity taxes, and partner loss carryovers, and it directs the Secretary to issue regulations to prevent avoidance. The amendment was ordered to lie on the table. CREC-SEL-01

Chair Alford described the bill as including nearly $18 billion for military construction and full funding for veterans' healthcare and benefits, while Ranking Member Wasserman Schultz stated opposition, citing increased community care funding, reduced funding for military construction relative to the President's request, and several riders. General debate was allotted one hour, equally divided. CREC-SEL-01

    Wosb Accountability Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-03 / CREC-2025-06-03-pt1-PgH2393

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 1816, the WOSB Accountability Act, on a motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended, introduced by Representatives McGarvey, Velazquez, and LaLota. The bill amends Section 15(g) of the Small Business Act so that only women-owned small business concerns certified under section 8(m)(2)(E) count toward specified governmentwide and agency goals, and it deems certain self-certified applicants certified for goal purposes until a determination is made. It requires the SBA Administrator to issue implementing regulations within one year, to provide quarterly briefings to the Small Business committees, and states that no additional funds are authorized.     FAPD-AI: Mr. Burchett moved to suspend the rules and pass H.R. 1998, the Sanction Sea Pirates Act of 2025, as amended.     Assessment of Trans-Atlantic Submarine Fiber Optic Cable (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-23 / CREC-2025-06-23-pt1-PgH2847

    FAPD-AI: Mr. Bilirakis moved to suspend the rules and pass H.R. 1737, which directs the Secretary of Commerce to submit a report to Congress within one year of enactment. The report would assess the value, cost, and feasibility of a trans-Atlantic submarine fiber optic cable connecting the contiguous United States, the United States Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria. Required elements include the lifespan and security of existing cables linking the Virgin Islands to the contiguous United States, telecommunications readiness in the Virgin Islands, and the feasibility of a data center and high-security cloud facility there for specified military and national security communications.   • Observed at 05:42:49 Eastern time ET
    Romance Scam Prevention Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-23 / CREC-2025-06-23-pt1-PgH2848

    FAPD-AI: Mr. Bilirakis moved to suspend the rules and pass H.R. 2481, the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which requires online dating service providers to send a fraud ban notification to any member who received a message from a banned member. Notifications must include the banned member's identifier, a statement that the banned member may be using a false identity or attempting fraud, a warning not to send cash or personal financial information, best-practice information, and customer service contact details, and must generally be provided within 24 hours of a fraud ban, with delays permitted in specified circumstances. The bill assigns enforcement to the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, preempts conflicting state notification requirements, and takes effect one year after enactment. CREC-SEL-01

    Global Investment in American Jobs Act of 2025 (opens in a new tab)

    FAPD-AI: Mr. Bilirakis moved to suspend the rules and pass H.R. 1679, the Global Investment in American Jobs Act of 2025, which directs the Secretary of Commerce and the Comptroller General of the Government Accountability Office to conduct an interagency review of United States competitiveness in attracting foreign direct investment from responsible private-sector entities based in trusted countries. The enumerated review topics include the economic impact of such investment, data localization and intellectual property barriers, and investments by State-owned or State-backed enterprises, including entities influenced by the Chinese Communist Party. The bill requires Federal Register notice and public comment, a report to Congress within one year of enactment, and excludes laws and policies relating to the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States from the review. Covered products include wipes marketed as baby or diapering wipes and household or personal care wipes composed partly or entirely of petrochemical-derived fibers that have significant potential to be flushed, and the bill sets placement, size, and contrast requirements while prohibiting representations that such products can or should be flushed. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the requirements, the bill preempts non-identical state labeling requirements, and it takes effect one year after enactment. CREC-SEL-01

    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-23 / CREC-2025-06-23-pt1-PgH2858

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 1520, the Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act, under a motion to suspend the rules and pass it. The bill prohibits a covered entity from determining that a qualified individual is ineligible for, denying, refusing to refer for, or refusing to place on a waiting list for an organ transplant or related services solely on the basis of disability, with an exception for disabilities that a physician finds medically significant after an individualized evaluation. It directs complaints to the HHS Office for Civil Rights and provides that it does not limit remedies under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The House considered H.R. 1082, the Shandra Eisenga Human Cell and Tissue Product Safety Act, under a motion to suspend the rules and pass it. The bill directs the HHS Secretary to support educational materials on organ, tissue, and eye donation, and amends section 368 of the Public Health Service Act to authorize civil penalties of $20,000 per violation, daily penalties after written notice, and an amount equal to the retail value of the affected products, with a total cap of $10,000,000 per proceeding. It also requires FDA to publish information on its Tissue Reference Group, establishment registrations and inspections, requires a public docket within 60 days of enactment, and requires a report to Congress by September 30, 2026.     FAPD-AI: Pages S3173-S3174 print the text of amendments SA 2278 through SA 2283 to S. 1582, the GENIUS Act, as submitted in the Senate on June 2, 2025. SA 2278 (Bennet) would define 'senior executive branch official' to include the President and Vice President; SA 2279 (Kennedy) would set Consumer Financial Protection Bureau employee pay under the General Schedule; and SA 2280 (Kennedy) would repeal section 704B of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. SA 2281 (Shaheen, Kaine, Welch, and Wyden) would exclude from International Emergency Economic Powers Act section 203 the authority to impose or increase duties or impose tariff-rate quotas; SA 2282 (Shaheen) would modify implementation of the Women, Peace, and Security Act of 2017; and SA 2283 (Shaheen) would add Title II, the 'Western Balkans Democracy and Prosperity Act.' CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Pages S3174-S3175 print amendment SA 2283 (Shaheen) to S. 1582, which adds Title II, the 'Western Balkans Democracy and Prosperity Act.' Its findings address economic and governance conditions, corruption, disinformation, cyber resilience, and dependence on Russian fossil fuels and natural gas in the seven Western Balkans countries, and cite the OSCE/ODIHR final report on Serbia's December 17, 2023 elections. Its sense-of-Congress provisions (Sec. 23) cover trade, investment, and European Union and NATO accession support, and its definitions (Sec. 24) define 'appropriate congressional committees,' 'ICT,' and 'Western Balkans.'     FAPD-AI: Senator Shaheen submitted amendment SA 2284 to S. 1582, a bill to provide for the regulation of payment stablecoins, and the amendment was ordered to lie on the table. The amendment adds Title II, the Mobilizing and Enhancing Georgia's Options for Building Accountability, Resilience, and Independence Act, which contains definitions, sense-of-Congress statements, and statements of U.S. policy toward the Republic of Georgia. It directs the Secretary of State to submit a classified report on Russian intelligence assets in Georgia within 180 days and a five-year bilateral strategy within 90 days, and it directs the President to determine within 90 days whether specified foreign persons have engaged in significant corruption or acts of violence or intimidation, with related inadmissibility and sanctions provisions.     253RD Anniversary of the "Gaspee" Raid (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-02 / CREC-2025-06-02-pt1-PgS3182-3

    FAPD-AI: Senator Whitehouse delivered remarks marking the 253rd anniversary of the Gaspee raid, recounting the June 1772 burning of the British naval schooner HMS Gaspee off the coast of Rhode Island. The remarks draw on Rory Raven's 'Burning the Gaspee' and Nick Bunker's 'An Empire on the Edge,' and the Senator requested that a December 14, 2023 Washington Post article on the Gaspee affair be printed in the Record. The article states that the Gaspee was burned in June 1772, about eighteen months before the Boston Tea Party, and that the British Crown offered a bounty for the participants, though no one came forward to provide information. CREC-SEL-01

    Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-11 / CREC-2025-06-11-pt1-PgH2625-5

    FAPD-AI: S. 331, the Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act, was called up in the House under House Resolution 489 for immediate consideration. The bill amends the Controlled Substances Act to place in schedule I any material containing a fentanyl-related substance, defined by specified structural modifications to fentanyl, and creates an alternative registration process for schedule I research. The text also directs the Department of Justice Inspector General to complete a study on research involving fentanyl within one year of enactment. CREC-SEL-01

    District of Columbia Federal Immigration Compliance Act of 2025 (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-11 / CREC-2025-06-11-pt1-PgH2634

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 2056, the District of Columbia Federal Immigration Compliance Act of 2025, was called up in the House under House Resolution 489, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute from the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. As amended, the bill provides that the District of Columbia may not have in effect any statute, ordinance, policy, or practice that prohibits or restricts District entities or officials from sharing citizenship or immigration status information or from complying with lawful Department of Homeland Security detainer requests under sections 236 or 287 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The bill was debated for one hour, with Representative Comer and Representative Lynch each controlling 30 minutes. CREC-SEL-01

    Providing for Consideration of H.R. 4, Rescissions Act of 2025 (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2025-06-11 / CREC-2025-06-11-pt1-PgH2639

    FAPD-AI: House Resolution 499 provides for consideration of H.R. 4, the Rescissions Act of 2025, under a closed rule with one hour of debate and one motion to recommit, and waives points of order against the bill. It states that section 1017 of the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 does not apply to bills introduced regarding the June 3, 2025 special message, and it adopts House Resolution 492. During floor debate, Representative Foxx urged support for the rule, and Representative McGovern opposed it, with both discussing the rescissions package and the reconciliation bill. CREC-SEL-01

    119 HR 9608 RH: Less Bureaucracy, Better Family Engagement Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr9608rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9608, the Less Bureaucracy, Better Family Engagement Act, was introduced July 9, 2026 by Mrs. Miller of Illinois, reported with an amendment on November 17, 2026 (Report No. 119-879), and referred to the Committee of the Whole House on the State of the Union. The bill would transfer to the Secretary of Health and Human Services the functions the Secretary of Education exercises under four programs: Family Engagement in Education Programs under part E of title IV of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, the Community Support for School Success program, the National Activities for School Safety program, and the Ready to Learn Programming Grant program. The bill also transfers related personnel, assets, contracts, and unexpended appropriations; directs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to ensure no net increase in full-time equivalent employees and to certify compliance; and sets out savings provisions for existing legal documents, pending proceedings, and suits, with the transfers taking effect six months after enactment and early implementation permitted before that date. BILLS-SEL-01

    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr4464rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 4464, the Preventive Health Savings Act, introduced July 16, 2025 by Mr. Obernolte and reported to the House on November 17, 2026, amends Section 202 of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 by adding subsection (h). Upon request by the budget and primary-jurisdiction committee leaders, the Director of the Congressional Budget Office must determine whether proposed legislation would produce net reductions in budget outlays in the budgetary outyears through preventive health care, and must include a description and estimate of any such reductions in projections on that legislation. Any such estimate is a supplementary estimate and may not be used to determine compliance with the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 or other budgetary enforcement controls. BILLS-SEL-01

    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr5525rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 5525, the Stop DC Capital Authoritarian Motorvehicle Enforcement and Restoration of Autonomy Act, introduced September 19, 2025 by Mr. Perry and reported with an amendment on November 17, 2026, repeals Title IX of the Fiscal Year 1997 Budget Support Act of 1996 and Section 103 of the Safety-Based Traffic Enforcement Amendment Act of 2012, which govern the District of Columbia's use of automated traffic enforcement systems. The bill also repeals Section 9e of the District of Columbia Traffic Act, 1925, which governs signage prohibiting certain right turns at red traffic signals. The bill's short title also permits citation as the Stop DC CAMERA Act. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 02:53:08 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 8801 RH: DC Rejecting Oppressive Automotive Driving Surcharges Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8801rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8801, the DC Rejecting Oppressive Automotive Driving Surcharges Act, introduced May 13, 2026 by Mr. Perry and reported with an amendment on November 17, 2026, prohibits the Council of the District of Columbia from enacting, and the Mayor from enforcing, any act, resolution, or requirement that imposes a congestion toll. The bill amends Section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to add enacting such a congestion toll to the list of prohibited actions. It defines a congestion toll as any charge for entry into or passing through a congestion tolling zone, and defines that zone as roadways, bridges, tunnels, approaches, or ramps located within or entering the District of Columbia. BILLS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9607, the Less Bureaucracy, Better Workforce Development Act, introduced July 9, 2026 by Mr. Walberg and reported with an amendment on November 17, 2026, transfers to the Secretary of Labor, acting through the Assistant Secretary of Labor for Employment and Training, the functions of the Department of Education's Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education. The transferred functions include those under the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act of 2006 (other than sections 116 and 117) and Title II of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, along with adult education and related programs. The bill directs the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to ensure no net increase in full-time equivalent employees at affected agencies, sets an effective date six months after enactment with early implementation permitted, and includes savings, suit-continuation, and reference-conforming provisions.     official summary: The Copyright Office is publishing a final rule establishing adjusted fees for registration, recordation, record retrieval, search and certification, the Licensing Section services, and other services. The Office last adjusted fees in 2020, based on a study of our fiscal 2016 and 2017 costs. Since that time, the costs of providing Office services have risen substantially due to inflation and other increases. The adjusted fees are intended to enable recovery of a percentage of the Office's costs, closer to historical levels, without imposing undue barriers to access its services. This rule will take effect January 5, 2027. FR-SEL-01

    Federal Register · govinfo API · CONSUMER PRODUCT SAFETY COMMISSION · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23435

    official summary: In September 2023, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC or Commission) issued a safety standard for button cell or coin batteries and consumer products containing such products in accordance with Reese's Law. The standard incorporated by reference ANSI/UL 4200A-2023, Standard for Safety for Products Incorporating Button Batteries or Coin Cell Batteries. UL Standards and Engagement (ULSE) has now issued a revised standard, ANSI/UL 4200A-2026. Consistent with Reese's Law, this direct final rule updates the mandatory safety standard to incorporate by reference ANSI/UL 4200A-2026. FR-SEL-01

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23437

    official summary: This action proposes to amend Class D surface airspace in Naples, FL, to properly contain instrument flight rule procedures. It also proposes to remove the Class E transition airspace extensions, as they are no longer necessary. Additionally, it proposes to reduce the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface, as updated instrument approach procedures have lessened the need for additional airspace. Finally, it proposes administrative updates to the airspace legal description. FR-SEL-02

    Takes of Marine Mammals Incidental to Specified Activities; Taking Marine Mammals Incidental to Military Readiness Acti… (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23450

    official summary: NMFS has received a request from the U.S. Department of the Navy (including the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Marine Corps; Navy) and on behalf of the U.S. Coast Guard (Coast Guard), U.S. Army (Army), and U.S. Air Force (Air Force) (hereafter, Navy, Coast Guard, Army, and Air Force are collectively referred to as the Action Proponents) for Incidental Take Regulations (ITR) and an associated Letter of Authorization (LOA) pursuant to the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA). The requested regulations would govern the authorization of take of marine mammals incidental to training and testing activities and modernization and sustainment of ranges conducted in the Mariana Islands Training and Testing (MITT) Study Area over the course of 7 years from July 2027 through July 2034. NMFS requests comments on this proposed rule. NMFS will consider public comments prior to making any final decision on the promulgation of the requested ITR and issuance of the LOA; agency responses to public comments will be summarized in the final rule, if issued. [official summary truncated; see source] FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23452

    official summary: The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters on the Mississippi River near New Orleans, LA. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the response to a vessel collision and sinking.   • Observed at 02:53:08 Eastern time ET
    Reserve Requirements of Depository Institutions (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · FEDERAL RESERVE SYSTEM · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23453

    official summary: The Board is amending Regulation D, Reserve Requirements of Depository Institutions, to reflect the annual indexing of the reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche for 2027. The annual indexation of these amounts is required notwithstanding the Board's action in March 2020 of setting all reserve requirement ratios to zero. The reserve requirement exemption amount for 2027 will remain $39.2 million, unchanged from 2026, consistent with the Federal Reserve Act (the “Act”). The Board is amending Regulation D to set the amount of the low reserve tranche at $688.5 million (increased from $674.1 million in 2026). The adjustment to the low reserve tranche is derived using a statutory formula specified in the Act. The annual indexation of the reserve requirement exemption amount and low reserve tranche is required by statute but will not affect depository institutions' reserve requirements, which will remain zero. FR-SEL-01

    Proposed QPAM Re-Eligibility Options After Disqualification (QROAD) Class Prohibited Transaction Exemption (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF LABOR · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23465

    official summary: This document gives notice of a proposed class prohibited transaction exemption (PTE). This proposed QROAD class PTE (Proposed QROAD Class Exemption) would allow certain qualified professional asset managers (QPAMs) to continue relying on PTE 84-14, known as the QPAM Class Exemption, even after an event that would otherwise make them ineligible under Section I(g) of that exemption. To use this alternative path, the QPAM must comply with the protective conditions in this Proposed QROAD Class Exemption, if granted. This proposal does not change any fiduciary duties under ERISA section 404 or expand the relief available under the QPAM Class Exemption. FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23475

    official summary: NMFS is prohibiting retention of Western and Central North Pacific Ocean (WCNPO) striped marlin ( Kajikia audax ) by vessels registered for use under a Hawaii longline limited access permit for the remainder of 2026 because the longline fishery has reached the 2026 longline retention limit. WCNPO stiped marlin are those caught in the Pacific Ocean north of the Equator (0° latitude) and west of 150° W longitude. This prohibition is intended to prevent the U.S. catch limit for WCNPO striped marlin from being exceeded and ensure compliance with NMFS regulations that implement decisions of the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC). FR-SEL-01

    Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-11-18 / 2026-23517

    official summary: Pursuant to the Federal Clean Air Act (CAA or Act), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve a State implementation plan (SIP) revision submitted by the Commonwealth of Virginia demonstrating that Virginia satisfies the interstate transport requirements of the CAA, for the 2010 1-hour sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) primary national ambient air quality standard (NAAQS). Specifically, the EPA proposes to find that the Virginia SIP contains adequate provisions prohibiting emissions from Commonwealth sources from contributing significantly to nonattainment or interfering with maintenance of the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS in any other State, consistent with the good neighbor provision of the CAA.     official summary: This document sets forth final regulations that provide guidance with respect to the automatic enrollment requirements that apply to certain retirement plans. The regulations reflect statutory changes made by the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 requiring that certain cash or deferred arrangements and salary reduction agreements be eligible automatic contribution arrangements that satisfy additional specified requirements. The regulations affect participants in, beneficiaries of, employers maintaining, and administrators of certain retirement plans that include cash or deferred arrangements or annuity contracts purchased under salary reduction agreements and other retirement plans that include eligible automatic contribution arrangements.     official summary: This document provides a notice of an additional date for the public hearing on the notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-119986-25) published in the Federal Register on Friday, September 4, 2026.
